title: A natural experiment on the effect of herpes zoster vaccination on dementia
source: Show notes (DOI only); episode discussion of Eyting et al., Nature 2025
one_line: Uses Wales's date-of-birth eligibility cutoff for the live zoster vaccine (Zostavax) as a natural experiment, comparing adults born just before versus just after 2 September 1933 to estimate the causal effect of vaccination on later dementia diagnoses.
key_claims: The birthdate cutoff created an abrupt, near-arbitrary jump in vaccine uptake between people differing in age by only weeks, supporting a regression-discontinuity causal design rather than a correlational comparison.

Eligibility for zoster vaccination reduced the probability of a new dementia diagnosis over a roughly 7-year follow-up, reported as about a 20% relative reduction among those who received the vaccine.
The protective association was larger in women than in men.
The discontinuity appeared for dementia but not for other tested health outcomes, arguing against generic healthy-vaccinee or health-seeking-behaviour confounding.
Findings are consistent with a hypothesis that suppressing varicella-zoster virus reactivation, or non-specific immune effects of a live vaccine, influences dementia risk.
limitations: Observational natural experiment on electronic health records, not a randomised trial, so residual confounding and diagnostic-coding error cannot be fully excluded.
Estimates are local to people born near the cutoff (around age 79-80 at eligibility) and may not generalise to other ages or populations.
Follow-up of about 7 years may be too short to capture longer-term effects or delayed diagnoses.
Dementia ascertainment relies on recorded diagnoses, which undercount and delay true onset.
The study concerns the live attenuated vaccine (Zostavax); it does not test the now widely used recombinant vaccine, and the mechanism was not directly interrogated.
open_questions: A randomised controlled trial of zoster vaccination with dementia incidence as a prespecified endpoint.
Does the recombinant subunit vaccine (Shingrix) produce the same effect, which would distinguish viral suppression from live-vaccine immune effects?
What explains the larger effect in women?
Do biomarkers (amyloid, tau, neuroinflammation) or VZV reactivation markers change after vaccination?
Does the effect persist or grow beyond 7 years of follow-up?
